raw_response:
Six mechanisms are worth considering. Their application to this Rust parser is an engineering inference; the dates below describe the evidence found, and none is a claim of deployment or demonstrated benefit.

1. **Rust macros by example expanding to patterns** — [Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/macros-by-example.html). A grammar-named macro that expands to a pattern can replace repeated nested match structure while keeping each match arm visibly aligned with its grammar rule. Parameterize the parts that vary and accept binding identifiers from callers. Hygiene and fragment composition matter. **Date status: unknown**; this live documentation does not establish availability on 2014-05-27.

2. **GHC parameterized pattern synonyms** — [versioned syntax-extension guide](https://downloads.haskell.org/ghc/7.8.1-rc1/docs/html/users_guide/syntax-extns.html). Named, parameterized patterns can hide repeated constructor structure and compose using grammar terminology. Matching-only forms suit structures that cannot be reconstructed uniquely; bidirectional forms also support construction. This is a language-design precedent for Rust. **Pre-cutoff evidence:** the [guide index](https://downloads.haskell.org/ghc/7.8.1-rc1/docs/html/users_guide/index.html) identifies version 7.8.20140130.

3. **Racket define-match-expander** — [Racket 5.3 reference](https://download.racket-lang.org/docs/5.3/html/reference/match.html). A named pattern transformer can translate concise grammar-shaped notation into ordinary patterns at expansion time, with an optional expression transformer for the same name. Transferring the mechanism requires Rust-specific binding and diagnostic rules. **Pre-cutoff evidence:** the [official release index](https://download.racket-lang.org/all-versions.html) dates Racket 5.3 to August 2012.

4. **Whole-match expression macros, illustrated by matches!** — [actual Rust core source](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/main/library/core/src/macros/mod.rs). When expression macros are available, a macro can own the complete match and package a recurring pattern and guard behind a grammar-named operation. The inspected matches! implementation returns a Boolean; a parser needing extracted bindings would need a custom success arm or returned value. This changes the visible layout of the match, so it fits best when the reusable unit is a recognition operation. **Later evidence:** [Rust 1.42.0 announcement](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2020/03/12/Rust-1.42/) dates stabilization to March 12, 2020.

5. **GHC view patterns, adapted as a Rust view function** — [versioned view-pattern documentation](https://downloads.haskell.org/ghc/7.8.1-rc1/docs/html/users_guide/syntax-extns.html). Move representation-specific deconstruction into a reusable function, then match grammar-named cases in its result. A Rust helper returning a borrowed view enum is a possible adaptation; it is not a claim that Rust supports GHC's view-pattern syntax. Check borrowing and repeated evaluation. **Pre-cutoff evidence:** the same guide version is dated 2014-01-30.

6. **Scala extractor objects using unapply** — [official specification changelog](https://www.scala-lang.org/files/archive/spec/2.11/15-changelog.html). A named extractor recognizes a value and returns its components, allowing a grammar production to be expressed independently of storage structure. A Rust helper returning Option of components offers an adaptation, although it lacks Scala's direct nesting syntax and needs careful treatment of effects and failure. **Pre-cutoff evidence:** the changelog dates extractors in Scala 2.3.2 to January 23, 2007.

The compile-time mechanisms preserve grammar-shaped patterns most directly. Whole-match macros provide an alternative expansion boundary. Views and extractors are useful when the recurring structure also hides a representation decision or requires computation.
